paras: The lynching of Hensley Johnson was the hanging of a Black man by a mob on the public square of Carthage, in Panola County, Texas, on the night of April 25, 1903. Johnson had been jailed on a charge of assaulting a four-year-old white girl and released on bond, and his body was found the next morning hanging from a telephone pole. A dispatch from Longview carried the story to papers across the country, while a correspondent to the Black paper Western World reported it under an editor's note calling the charge "a lie on its face."

According to the Longview dispatch, Johnson was accused of criminally assaulting a four-year-old white girl of Carthage on the Friday night before the lynching. Officers of Panola County captured him and placed him in jail, but he was released on bond on Saturday, April 25.

After his release Johnson "left for the country," where a mob from Carthage captured him that night. The mob hanged him on the public square, and on the morning of April 26 his body was found suspended from a telephone pole. In the dispatch's account, the mob "was quiet" and the people of Carthage knew nothing of the lynching until the body was discovered.
No report of an inquest, arrests, a grand jury inquiry or a trial appears in the coverage.

Most white papers ran a Longview dispatch of April 26, credited by the Butte Inter Mountain to the Associated Press, which appeared the next day in the New-York Tribune, the Birmingham Age-Herald, the Savannah Morning News and others. The versions handled the accusation differently: the Age-Herald, the Morning News and the Courier-Journal printed that he "criminally assaulted" the child, the Tribune and the Kennebec Journal said "it is alleged," and the Wheeling Register and the Minneapolis Journal said he was "charged with" it. Headlines ranged from "Negro Lynched in Texas" to the Kennebec Journal's "Negro Ravisher Quickly Disposed of," and the Pickens Sentinel-Journal in South Carolina headed its version "Lynched for the Usual Crime" with the subhead "The Well-deserved Fate of a Brute." Condensed versions ran in news digests and weeklies from Nevada to South Carolina into mid-May.

Southern editors paired the case with the lynching the same weekend at Thebes, Illinois, where the mob went on to attack a company of Black workers. The Raleigh News and Observer found "no sectionalism in race prejudices or in determination to punish rape swiftly," a paragraph the Richmond Times Dispatch reprinted. Two days later the same paper asserted that "in Texas the offending negro was lynched after his guilt had been ascertained" and that the Texas mob "had no resentment against negroes as such." The Lexington Dispatch in South Carolina, quoting the Spartanburg Herald, counted the Texas hanging among four "outrages" against Black people that spring and took pride that only one had occurred in the South.

In the Black press, an item datelined Carthage, April 29, in the Western World named the victim as "Henry Jenninson, 18 years old," said he was lynched "Sunday morning," and reported only that "it is claimed" he tried to assault a four-year-old girl. Below it the editor added: "The suspect charge is a lie on its face." That summer the Wichita Searchlight, the Seattle Republican, in a list headed "Mobocracy's Bloody Reign," and the Sedalia Times, reprinting a record kept by The Striker, entered the case in their tallies of the year's lynchings.

The girl's age was given as four in the full dispatch and in the Western World, as five in the Minneapolis Journal, and as fourteen in the Butte Inter Mountain and the Lincoln County Record. The victim's name appeared as Hensley Johnson, Hensely John, Henley Johnson and Henry Johnson in white papers, and as Henry Jenninson in the Western World. The dispatch placed the lynching on Saturday night; the Pickens Sentinel-Journal's rewrite said Friday night, the Western World Sunday morning, and the Black-press lists April 26. Whether Johnson committed the assault was stated as fact by some white papers, called alleged by others and denied by the Western World's editor, and no account reports any hearing on the charge.

reader.title: Lynching of Hensley Johnson
bases: A mob from Carthage seized Johnson after his release on bond and hanged him on the public square (A7, A6, A23).

Every account calls the killers a mob, which captured Johnson in the country and hanged him without legal authority (A7, A6, A23); the papers tie the hanging to the charge of assaulting a white child (A7, A22).

The Longview wire dispatch (A7, A6, A9) and an independent Carthage item in the Black paper Western World (A23) agree that he was lynched at Carthage on a charge of assaulting a four-year-old girl; they differ on his name and the hour.

accounts.label: Longview wire dispatch
accounts.gist: News reached Longview on April 26 that a mob from Carthage had captured Johnson in the country after his release on bond and hanged him on the public square; the mob was quiet and the town learned of it when the body was found.

accounts.label: Black correspondent at Carthage
accounts.gist: 'Henry Jenninson, 18 years old' was lynched Sunday morning; 'it is claimed' he tried to assault a four-year-old girl, a charge the editor called a lie.

accounts.label: Raleigh News and Observer editorial
accounts.gist: Claimed the Texas mob lynched the man 'after his guilt had been ascertained' and harmed no other Black people, unlike the Illinois mob.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Longview dispatch under headlines such as 'Negro Lynched in Texas', some stating the assault as fact and others calling it 'alleged' or 'charged'.
Pickens Sentinel-Journal: 'Lynched for the Usual Crime. The Well-deserved Fate of a Brute'; Kennebec Journal: 'Negro Ravisher Quickly Disposed of'.
Raleigh News and Observer used the case to argue that Southern lynching punished guilt while Northern mobs attacked Black people indiscriminately.
Lexington Dispatch, quoting the Spartanburg Herald, counted the hanging among 'outrages' against Black people while defending the South.
Western World's editor called the charge 'a lie on its face'; later Black papers listed the case in tallies headed 'Mobocracy's Bloody Reign' and 'Record of Lynching'.
